newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK's Tung says world misunderstands planned changes.
newsitem.headline: HK's Tung says world misunderstands planned changes.

text.p: Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, said on Tuesday that the international community did not understand China's proposed changes in the territory's human rights laws.

"There are negative impacts because many news reports are negative and misleading. I think we need to spend more time to explain to them (the international community). Gradually, they will understand," Tung told reporters after emerging from the first meeting of his cabinet.

Tung said an informal meeting of his Executive Council on Tuesday discussed the decision by a China-appointed committee last Saturday to roll back civil liberties laws after Hong Kong is handed back to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.
But he did not elaborate on whether he and his advisers had reached a conclusion on how to tackle the issue, which has sparked an outcry in Hong Kong and from the world community.
Hong Kong Chief Secretary Anson Chan, who will stay on as Tung's deputy beyond the handover, highlighted the problem on Monday night on her return from a trip to the United States.
"I have to say that the (decision) concerning the Bill of Rights Ordinance and repeal of legislation had sent an extremely negative signal to people in America," Chan told reporters.

During the Executive Council meeting, protesters from the Democratic Party, the territory's largest, presented a petition with more than 20,000 signatures to an aide of the Chief Executive-designate protesting changes on the human rights laws.
"I think Hong Kong people have to speak up and show our discontent," group spokesman Mak Hoi-wah told reporters. "I think the move is detrimental to human rights in Hong Kong."
Tung said he and his inner cabinet discussed procedures and structure of the council during Monday's meeting, and agreed to start regular weekly meetings from February 18.
The future Hong Kong leader also said he had received confidential files on the colonial government's top officials ahead of deciding on who would stay on past the handover.
"I have now with me the information on the top officials. After I finish with them...I will give them back to the government," he said.

Chinese officials on Monday reiterated demands that the files be handed over to Beijing, while British officials have maintained the issue was strictly between the present and future Hong Kong administrations.
